#4040. Talking Point: As A Parent, What Worries You Most About Gaming?

Nintendo's guide aims to highlight the benefits

Over the summer, I replayed Ocarina of Time (1998) with my kids. I hadn't intended to, but it dawned on me that once the gorgeous remake landed, the original's visible polygons might not hold the same appeal for them. It was selfish, really, but I wanted them to experience the original magic as I did.

I held the pad but let them direct me, staying silent or feigning ignorance about puzzle solutions, letting them speculate and point out chests and switches I'd intentionally run past, involving them in an adventure they don't quite have the dexterity to control themselves.

I worried their attention might wander while watching for 30-60 minutes at a time, and I don't want to be that parent, forcing something I loved on my disinterested kids ("What do you mean 'Thunderbirds is boring'?!"). I was ready to pull the cord if they didn't take to it.

But no! They were pointing and problem-solving alongside me, jumping up and down, utterly engaged and loving the story and our shared experience.

Beyond the screen, Ocarina provoked laughter over dinner, and discussion about why characters reacted as they did, the cause and effect of actions, and the resulting emotions. Car journeys suddenly had a new soundtrack accompaniment, and the game's themes would come up while drawing or playing with Lego or finding a 'Deku' stick out on a walk. It became a rich source of inspiration for their imaginations, and a springboard to conversation and closeness with my kids. A fantastic family adventure we'll remember for years to come.

It's such a shame, then, when you see parents whose kids love games struggle to recognise the benefits and sheer joy they can bring, and potentially miss out on family experiences like mine. For something so ubiquitous and so fun, gaming can create real tension in the home and throw up generational barriers that take time and understanding to break down.

And with all the online concerns and other ills of the modern age, it's easy to see why some parents might perceive games as a dead-end, dangerous time sink that needs to be contained and quarantined, like fast food or social media.

According to a recent Ofcom report, 88% of children aged 3-17 in the UK play games on some form of device, and given Nintendo's evergreen, all-ages remit to deliver surprise and delight, addressing concerns of gaming-cautious guardians is something the company is keen on, beyond the bare minimum of secure account systems and Parental Control tools.

So that'll be why they've partnered up with Andy Robertson, founder of the Family Gaming Database and longtime friend of the site, for the recently published Parent's Guide to Gaming with Confidence.

Longtime Nintendo Life readers may recognise Andy from the various articles and reviews he's penned for us over the years, or from our partnership with Family Gaming to highlight accessibility information in our reviews and game pages across the network.

Produced in association with Nintendo, in this new guide Andy has also enlisted other experts in the fields of gaming, child psychology, and online safety to help parents of all gaming backgrounds digest the key questions and perhaps reframe how some of them view video games.

The prevalence of online gaming and voice chat worries me a lot. I don't want my kid speaking to strangers or picking up bad language or habits. Everything is so much easier (and tempting) to access than it used to be!

Available as a downloadable PDF, Andy explores common misconceptions and offers sound advice from expert contributors, including child psychologist Dr Amanda Gummer and Dr Catherine Knibbs, a child and adult psychotherapist specialising in online harm.

As you'll see from the breakout boxes on this page, uncertainties about other online players and predatory monetisation systems are the main sources of anxiety for NL staff with kids. "I'm very concerned about exploitative mechanics," says Alex, our senior video producer, "things designed to get their hooks into people's brains and make them dependent, or cough up wads of cash."

According to Ofcom's research, these are common worries:

The biggest type of concern among parents and carers of 3-17-year-olds who play games online is their child talking to strangers through games or via the chat functions (64%). This is followed by concerns about bullying by other players (60%), exposure to inappropriate content such as violence, bad language or disturbing material (59%), and pressure to make in-game purchases (51%).

Dr Knibbs highlights how "digital spaces can feel less familiar" than physical play spaces like playgrounds. The dangers can be less obvious, too, although she stresses that understanding the risks is better than avoidance. "When we learn about the content, the people and the spaces our children are engaging with, we are much better placed to help them navigate those experiences safely and positively."

It's not just about risk assessment, but also realising the potential benefits - and that doesn't require extensive gaming experience. "The goal ISN’T to become a gamer," Andy writes. "It is to better understand the people you care about most." You don't need to have conquered Elden Ring or any other game to participate and 'get' games.

Games with random or chance-based outcomes, especially with microtransactions that encourage you to spend money and try again, are what concern me most. As much as I enjoy it, Pokémon GO is a strong example of this (there’s a reason it was recently bumped up to PEGI 16), but thankfully, there are enough single-player adventures out there (Pokémon included!) that can minimise these often frustrating and FOMO-driven elements for younger players.

Another key point to stress to non-gaming parents might seem almost self-evident, but it's easily overlooked if recognising Mario and Pac-Man represents your sum knowledge of the medium.

For some, even now, 'gaming' remains an arcade-style competition for high scores, and that can create a disconnect between parents with preconceived notions and their kids, who are discovering that games can be so much more.

"A child who is creating, collaborating, problem-solving or connecting with friends is having a very different experience from someone passively consuming content," Dr Amanda Gummer writes in a section of the guide highlighting "one of the most common mistakes parents make" - that all games are essentially the same.

We can all recall 'Wow, games can do this???' moments when the scales fell from our eye. It might have been an emotional beat in Shadow of the Colossus, or a surprising Wii Sports session with grandparents over the holidays; whatever the source, getting the uninitiated to that point is a crucial first step. While it's all notionally 'reading', hopping between Wikipedia articles is obviously not the same as reading a poem or sitting down with James Patterson's latest or doomscrolling social media feeds or taking a crack at Ulysses, and once parents understand that the world of video games is equally expansive, they've got a foundation to build upon.

Andy takes time to break down what he terms "the myth of the isolated gamer" and how, in fact, games can bring families together. Living the Nintendo life as we do, multiplayer has been commonplace for decades, but the lone gamer in the basement/attic stereotype persists.

Likewise — and this has long been a personal bugbear when talking with friends and family — rationing 'screen time' feels like an oversimplification for parents guarding against passive media consumption. Lamenting how young people these days don't get enough fresh air is absolutely valid, and getting out in the park, playground, and beyond is crucial to a child's overall development, but it's not as simple as 'outside=good, inside=bad'. The storytelling, learning, collaboration, creativity, and deep experiences games can offer are enormously valuable.

As Andy points out, "understanding the quality of the experience is often more useful than simply counting the minutes." Bowling in Switch Sports, having the national news on in the background, diving into a Mario world, and throwing Bluey on Disney+ are all different types of 'screen time', each with their own benefits and potential drawbacks.

You may not have noticed, but Nintendo Life has grown recently. Behind the scenes, we've had new additions to the family, with two team members recently joining the ranks of Hookshot Media parentdom.

Across our editorial, video, and management teams, our collective tribe runs the age gamut from newborn to undergrad, so we've got a broad range of experience, making it fairly simple to gauge what's appropriate for our kids, suggest games they might like (or slyly leave them lying around to be 'discovered') while monitoring interactions and steering them towards the all-timers (hi, Ocarina) and, importantly, away from less healthy, obsessive patterns that we may have fallen into in our youth.

And yes, there are certain games, primarily targeting younger gamers, that we wouldn't install on any device in the house.

I don’t worry too much about microtransactions as I will maintain strict control over any potential in-game purchases. However, I dread the day that my daughter gets roped into playing something like Roblox. Substantial, well-made games can offer a lot of value for children, but Roblox is not an example of this.

Authorities in some territories are taking steps to mitigate the potential harm of the aggressive monetisation systems baked into platforms like Roblox. In the last week, the EU published its Digital Fairness Act proposal, which could impact any game featuring in-game purchases in the EU. Among other things, the bloc is seeking to curtail "addictive design", "dark patterns", and predatory monetisation tactics.

The DFA would only affect players in Europe, but regulation that forces real currency prices and lootbox odds to be displayed, those and similar systems defaulting to 'off' for minors, and parental consent being required to activate them are all positive steps.

While legislation could mean big changes for some developers and publishers, it's unlikely to cause Nintendo itself headaches.

With first-party software, in-game purchases are typically limited to DLC expansions or Switch 2 Upgrade Packs, and content-wise, it's a rare Nintendo game that I wouldn't feel comfortable playing with my kids in the room - something our teams over on Push Square and Pure Xbox have to be more cautious about, I'd wager.

My child is too young to play games on their own yet, but we’re having a blast with Mario Kart World’s Free Roam mode. It’s perfect, honestly: beyond the vibrant, fun characters, and chancing upon helicopters, lorries, and UFOs you can play as, seeing them gradually understand the geography of this vast world as you string one P-Switch mission to the next has made one of my favourite ever Mario Kart (and gaming) experiences.

Every kid is different, of course. Some may not be phased at all by a lurching ReDead in Hyrule Castle Town, while others might be kept up at night after glimpsing a creepy icon on the home screen. Handily, Switch's handheld hybrid format does make it easier to take the game away from the living room if, say, you need half an hour with Resident Evil Requiem away from eager eyes, and the console's aforementioned Parental Controls and accompanying app make monitoring the kids' gaming pretty simple.

Communicating to nervous parents not just the risks but the rewards is something we're passionate about on the team, and that's something that Andy's guide does particularly well. "Failure is a part of success," he writes. "Games create safe environments where mistakes are expected. This can help children build resilience without even realising it. Every setback becomes part of learning." Makes me feel better about all the times the dogs got me in Call of Duty.

Gaming with an infant is… difficult! (Try explaining that Fortune's Weave isn't touchscreen to a five-month-old). But I genuinely can't wait until my child is old enough to participate; as cheesy as it is, I think I'm going to well up when she picks her first starter Pokémon.

Confidence is a key term. Naturally, it's in Nintendo's interest to maintain its carefully curated family-friendly image, but giving parents who aren't embedded in the ins and outs of the gaming scene the confidence to engage is a win for the medium and everyone who loves it. A digestible guide like this for game-sceptic family and friends could come in handy over the holidays.

(To be clear, I'm not advocating becoming a gaming missionary at the dinner table and forcing pamphlets on relatives. But, you know, slyly leaving them lying around to be 'discovered' and having Switch Sports Resort ready to go after dessert? A round of golf and some bowling has worked wonders in the past!)

As with anything, a good grasp of the issues is essential, and every parent and child will have their own approaches, preferences, and ideas. For the NL team, though — and for me personally — sharing how games can enrich our family lives regardless of experience and ability is important. By alleviating concerns and highlighting benefits, we can open doors for new players and experience more of those treasured 'Oh, games can do this???' moments together.

What worries you most as a parent? Which games have you played and enjoyed the most with your kids? Let us know your thoughts in the polls below, and feel free to take to the comments to share your experiences and the effect gaming has in your family.

Gavin first wrote for Nintendo Life in 2018 before joining the site full-time the following year, rising through the ranks to become Editor. He can currently be found squashed beneath a Switch backlog the size of Normandy.

Hang on... how does Chess have more kids using it than Fortnite? I think that's a good thing

What worries me most about gaming is how companies are employing people to prey on addictions as part of their design philosophies. That extends to Gambling (loot boxes, gacha, etc), FOMO, Dark Patterns, and anything else that falls under the commerce-driven psychological manipulation category.

As a father of two cats, I’m concerned about the addictiveness of games. When Pokémon is on the big screen, they’re barely able to distinguish fiction from reality. Deeply worrying stuff.

Personally, I’m glad Roblox is not on Switch.

Too many stories, too much to go wrong with young children.

My wife and I don't have kids yet, but we talk a lot about how we're going to implement gaming into our home with our future children. I grew up playing games extensively, and she only grew up playing Just Dance on the Wii and a handful of games on the DS. I've gotten her into gaming recently, and she's really loving it (especially the new OoT Remake) because she didn't know that modern gaming was so much more than Call of Duty.

The thing I'm most worried about for our future kids is endless, meaningless games-as-a-service games, like Roblox and Fortnite. There's no story, no curation, and/or no purpose. You end up consuming slop over and over, and you gain nothing. We plan on being very careful with the games we bring into our home so it adds to their lives the same way the artwork you choose to hang on your walls and the music you play in your home can shape their views of the world and influence who they become.

Not a parent, but I have spent a lot of time around my nieces and nephews and have watched the games they play. They all play Roblox to some extent (it’s even on their parents’ and grandparents’ iPads, and they’re constantly asking for screens whenever they visit family). My biggest concerns with them and gaming for younger audiences in general are the predatory nature of the games and the lack of concern for their safety from almost all involved parties.

The first point is simple: from what I’ve seen, games on Roblox are meant to be as addictive as possible. By getting kids hooked, they’ll want to keep coming back for more. They do this by having instant feedback loops where you feel like you’re accomplishing something great by ticking up a number constantly. And by implementing the cosmetics and currencies, they’ll be tempted to ask for money for Robux. It just feels predatory.

The last part is on the games, but also on parents. I don’t want to say my siblings are not parenting well, but they’re not gamers, so to me, they don’t seem to be monitoring what their kids consume. And Roblox, as we’ve heard in recent news, can be a breeding ground for predators. It feels way too easy for kids to have access to people they can chat with, and unless a parent is actively monitoring every person they chat to, they don’t know if the person on the other end has good motives.

I don’t want to act like online gaming can’t be helpful for kids, and honestly, kids should be able to play online with their friends. But I think it requires a lot more vigilance from their parents. Long gone are the days where an iPad could babysit a kid (a practice I didn’t even like back when iPads were first introduced). Parents need to have an active role in their kids’ development rather than trusting that the media their kids consume will be good for them.

The online stuff is the worry in the main - but that is just the same stuff that is bothersome about the internet generally.

I know what my daughter is playing and will keep it that way for as long as possible.

As a personal note, i don't have kids but i used to be one. For some reason this article made me feel nostalgic so excuse the rambling.

My parents never really got gaming. Instead my parents watched movies with me. I remember my dad showing me Star Wars Episode 1 and telling him that Jar Jar was my favorite, he never showed me the rest of the movies. Also Austin Powers at an age where most of the dirty jokes flew over my head but it's probably part of the reason why i love stupid dirty jokes.

As a not-parent, I don't like lootboxes. In general. They're just bad.

Mostly who my kids may be talking to and loot boxes, so I watch my kids play games or play with them as much as I can. But, if I'm honest, I understand gaming very well and what my kids "should" play. I don't worry a lot about what they play because I pay for it and I know what I'm buying since I'm not 80.

As someone who has raised two kids who are now older teens and gamed their entire life here are my tips:

1. Dictate everything they can play. The likes of Roblox might be predatory but they are also utter balls. That play time is only so high because non-gaming parents use it to keep their kids quiet. You’re already on a Nintendo site and therefore know better. Let them play the classics you grew up with. The best thing you can do for your kids is curate taste in video games.

2. Play with them as much as possible. Get the Wii out the loft and play some Resort with them. If they’re a bit older try some co-op titles. Secret of Mana remains a milestone to this day. If they’re want to play shooters put paintball mode on Perfect Dark and do co-op vs bots.

3. Take time to listen to what they’re interested in as they age. If you’ve done your job right (see part 1) they’ll want to talk to you about games. My youngest is always throwing crazy Zelda theories at me that sound like 2000 era forum posts and it’s wonderful.

4. Play games as a family on a regular basis. Sit down and play Bomberman or Mario Kart together once a week.

As the father of a four-year-old girl and a one-year-old boy, I care deeply about teaching my children never to become blindly loyal to any brand—not even when it comes to something as personal and entertaining as video games.

I want them to understand the importance of maintaining their bargaining power as consumers and never becoming easy targets of marketing campaigns, whether obvious or subtle, designed to trigger emotional responses and drive impulse purchases.

Just because they may grow up enjoying a privileged lifestyle doesn't mean they should buy things without stopping to consider what those products are actually worth. That kind of judgment requires reason, not emotion.

This doesn't mean raising them to be cold or detached people. Quite the opposite: I want them to be loving, warm, and fun. But when it comes to consuming, I want them to be rational, independent, and deliberate.

Our family didn't get to where it is by spending money carelessly, and I want my children to understand that.

#4039. Three Classic Startup Animations Are Rolling Out Today On Xbox (November 15)

It's official! These animations are now rolling out to all players on Xbox One, Series X and Series S:

Original Story: So, you remember that recent Xbox console update we mentioned yesterday? The one that happened on Wednesday and included original Xbox achievements? It seems like there's at least one more hidden feature to be discovered.

A couple of eagle-eyed Xbox fans have spotted that the patch notes had been adjusted for this update last night, and they mentioned that three classic startup animations were being added to "celebrate 25 years of Xbox history".

The three animations are for the original Xbox, Xbox 360 (2005) and Xbox 360 (2010).

Since then, the patch notes have been adjusted once more to just reference "miscellaneous" improvements, so it seems like they jumped the gun slightly and were supposed to wait until November 15th (the date of Xbox's 25th anniversary) to reveal these three startup animations.

None of them are live yet by the way, but it might be worth checking the "Startup" section of your Xbox console's Settings menu periodically over the next couple of days to see if they show up.

I don't know about you, but I'm going to be rocking the original Xbox startup animation as soon as possible!

Here's a look at what you can expect from the three animations when they become available:

Poll Which Xbox Startup Animation Will You Pick In The New Console Update?

It's with Insiders right now, but will soon become totally public

Excited for these classic Xbox startup animations? Let us know down in the comments section below.

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

#4038. GTA 6 Ultimate Edition DLC Won’t Be Permanent Or Immediately Accessible

Despite all the controversy surrounding its expensive DLC edition and discless release, Grand Theft Auto 6 has been absolutely smashing just about every review record out there, with countless new gameplay details and footage going live now that its staggered regional release has started. While most of the responses have been glowing so far, a few details still haven't gone over well with fans.

Although the high price didn't deter many players, at least if its pre-release sales figures are anything to go by, early player reports have been noting that several of the in-game content offered by GTA 6's deluxe edition aren't as permanent as they first sounded.

On top of the $100 price tag, early sources like Pirat_Nation have claimed that much of the content included in GTA 6's deluxe edition won't be available from the start. Requiring you to progress past certain points in the story to access them, certain mechanics like limited vehicles, stores, and customization options will take a bit of effort to unlock.

While progression locking the DLC already has some fans disgruntled, the part that has fans most frustrated is that several inclusions in the DLC will supposedly only be available for certain chapters, like Jason's Dinka Enduro Motorcycle, Low Riding Pickup, and Crest Kayak that can only be used in the very first chapter of the game before seemingly losing access to them again.

While these changes likely won't detract much from Grand Theft Auto 6's glowing review scores, another concern fans have been raising comes from the GTA+ subscription service benefits that New Zealand players have been sharing online, which seemingly grant other in-game rewards and exclusive content in exchange for a paid monthly fee.

While the content offered by GTA+ isn't exactly game-changing and mostly offers bonuses like passive discounts or sale increases, it does also provide a free racecar and garage for players to use, offering a significant advantage to start off with compared to players who simply purchase the base game, or even its deluxe edition.

#4037. Cleanser Man Is Mega Man: Dual Override’s Boss Design Contest Winner

Mega Man: Dual Override’s 2025 reveal brought back the classic boss design contest, asking fans to create and submit their own robot masters, with Capcom choosing one to include in the game. After thousands of submissions, we have our winner; meet Cleanser Man.

As his name suggests, Cleanser Man is a cleaning robot who attacks (and tidies) using a long, multi-cleaning hose arm. Capcom has provided the following character summary:

Cleanser Man is a cleaning robot with an obsession for pristine beauty. Fueled by an extremely sensitive dirt sensor, Cleaner Man’s ideal world is one without a speck of dust. However, his devotion to cleanliness has a cost. His aggressive scrubbing causes great damage to global landmarks and historic works of art. This fixation has caused the public to view him as more of a threat than a helping hand. Furious and feeling misunderstood, Cleanser Man seizes control of trash processing facility and uses it to pollute the environment with hopes of forcing the world to appreciate the importance of cleanliness.

Cleanser Man won out among the six finalists, a few of which were also cleaning-themed bosses. “In the end, we chose Cleanser Man because of the unique way the concept was brought together and the originality of the color design,” says game director Shinya Ikuta. “While staying true to and respecting the original submission, we adjusted certain details to better fit the world and style of the game.”  Unfortunately, Capcom has not revealed Cleanser Man's creator, but you can see the character in action in the reveal video below.

In addition to Cleanser Man, Mega Man: Dual Override's rogues' gallery includes the following revealed robot masters: Twinkle Girl, Jet Man, Tank Man, and Cook Man. The remaining three bosses have yet to be revealed.

Mega Man: Dual Override launches in 2027 for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Switch, and PC.  To learn more about the game, read our extended preview here. You can also check out the game's recently revealed amiibo figures for the Switch versions.

#4035. 2027 Video Game Grammy Nominations Include Avatar: Frontiers Of Pandora For The Third Time

Since 2023, the Recording Academy has included an official category for video game soundtracks, adding an air of legitimacy to a diverse musical medium we know and love. Today, we learned the list of nominees for the 2027 Grammy ceremony, and it's an interesting lineup. The nominations are as follows:

As is often the case, what stands out most about these nominees is how, generally speaking, they don't fully align with gaming culture's favorite soundtracks of the year, and instead often trend toward the most recognizable IP (often franchises with films) of the year. On that note, it's most surprising to see that Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora has been nominated for the third year in a row: once for the base game, once for the Secrets of the Spires DLC, and now for the From The Ashes DLC. None of these soundtracks are bad by any means, but their Grammy representation far outweighs their cultural footprint.

The standout here is Ghost of Yōtei, which is not an adaptation of the massive franchises the other games fall into. However, it's also a Sony-published game, which have a pretty good track record of getting nominations, potentially due to the company's massive presence in the music and film industries. Still, Ghost of Yōtei has a great, unique score that's deserving of its spot, and also one previously nominated for best music at the 2025 Game Awards. The Grammys accept any releases between October 1 of one year and September 30 of the following year, so Ghost of Yōtei barely made the cut for this window. The Game Awards nominees will be announced tomorrow – it will be interesting to see how much overlap there is between the categories.

This batch of Grammy noms also has fewer recurring nominees than past years. This is Gordy Haab's third nomination (he won in 2024 for Star Wars Jedi: Survivor) and John Paesano's second nomination (he was nominated in 2025 for Marvel's Spider-Man 2). It's also the first year since the awards' creation without Bear McCreary or Austin Wintory nominations.

Last year's nominations left a sour taste in the mouths of many, with several DLC nominees and a complete lack of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, the year's standout hit that many specifically praised for its music. This year certainly has snubs (Mewgenics, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, and Control Resonant all come to mind), but none as egregious as last year.

What do you think was the best video game score from the last year? Let us know in the comments!

#4034. All the hype has already made Crimson Desert one of the biggest launches on Steam this year

We're merely days away from the end of the first quarter of 2026, and Crimson Desert has come in clutch to join the list of big sellers.

Crimson Desert, the open-world action RPG off-shoot from Korean MMO Black Desert Online, has officially launched, nearly six years after it was initially revealed. The game has been building up a lot of momentum over the years, which recently coalesced to turn it into one of 2026’s most anticipated titles.

All of it has been leading up to this moment, and the game appears to have landed smoothly, though not without controversy, as has seemingly become part of its MO.

It has not been 24 hours since Crimson Desert launched on PC and consoles, and it’s already become a big hit. On Steam, one of two stores where the game can be purchased (the other being the Epic Games Store), the game shot to the top of the charts.

The action RPG continued to accumulate more and more players on Steam, peaking at a very respectable 239,045 concurrent players (via SteamDB). Though its success was very much expected, we perhaps didn’t predict its peak would be that high.

Indeed, Crimson Desert has been in Steam’s top 100 global sellers list for six weeks, jumping up six spots to become the number one seller this week just before it launched. As we get closer to the weekend, the numbers could climb even higher.

This peak concurrent puts Crimson Desert in the same league as several of the other major releases of the first quarter of 2026. The top spot continues to belong to Slay the Spire 2, which peaked at a staggering 574,638 concurrent players. It happened just days after the juggernaut Resident Evil Requiem achieved its own 344,214 peak concurrent, which was the year’s highest up until Slay the Spire 2’s release. All three are well ahead of Nioh 3’s 88,045 peak concurrent, and Marathon’s nearly identical peak of 88,337.

Crimson Desert has seen something of a mixed reception by critics. James gave it three stars in our review, saying it “lacks the connective sinew to be truly functional,” which is a common criticism shared by other outlets. Many also lamented the sheer number of systems fighting for player attention, its poorly explained mechanics, and counterintuitive controls.

On Steam, at least, players have similarly been divided, with the current Steam user rating sitting at Mixed, based on 8,728 reviews. Unsurprisingly, most of the negative reactions fall on the clunky controls and the game’s tendency to, as one Steam user put it, “so miserably tries to be everything at once, and fails to be anything at all.”

#4033. Make Room For GTAVI By Deleting Your PS5 Trophy Clips

Hard drive space is a premium commodity, and its value has never been more apparent than in the approximately two and a half days leading up to the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. The game is a whopping 209 GB, but thankfully you can purchase the game and preload it now – which you should do because who knows if the servers are going to be able to handle the strain of what is officially the most pre-ordered game ever on both PlayStation and Xbox platforms.

The easy (and likely necessary) answer is to delete the big games you aren't currently playing off your hard drive, but there is a cache of arguably unnecessary data on PlayStation 5 that might get you there before you have to make hard decisions.

You may have turned it off (Settings > Capture and Broadcasts > Captures > Trophies under the Auto-captures section > Save Trophy Videos under the Video Clips section > Change to None), which if that is the case, then I'm sorry. I can't help you. But the default setting which maybe you've never touched, is saving a lot of unnecessary video.

Every time you get a Trophy on PlayStation 5, it creates a short video clip that I bet you never have and never will watch. Here's how to delete all those videos fairly quickly to free up at least some space.

First up, go to the Media Gallery. The quickest way to do that is to press the screenshot button to the left of the touchpad, tap over to the most recent media capture on the left, press X, and then press the Go to Media Gallery button.

Next, go to the Trophies tab, go to the Sort and Filter option (the downward arrow with the three lines), and change Media Type to Video Clips.

After that, go back a few screens and go to the Select Multiple option (the overlapping squares with the check mark on it). Go ahead and press the Select All option, then press Delete, and then hold your breath and commit by pressing Delete again.

In taking screenshots to write this little article, I deleted 110 14-second clips. That's about 25 minutes of video footage, which ain't nothing. Maybe it will help you not delete that one game that you started three years ago that you are definitely going to get back to any day now.

#4032. Guide: GTA 6 Release Times: All The Key Details Xbox Players Need To Know

It's finally here! We've officially reached the launch week of GTA 6 on Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, PS5 and even the Xbox One (kind of), 13 long years since the most recent entry in the series back in 2013.

With that in mind, we thought we'd put up a quick release times guide so you know exactly when you can start playing the game, and we've also thrown in a few extra details about what we're expecting for Xbox One players at launch.

So, here are all the deets you need to know for Thursday!

On this page: GTA 6 Release Times: All The Key Details Xbox Players Need To Know

The official GTA 6 release date is Thursday, November 19th. You may still see people playing it on Wednesday though, as depending on where you live, certain players will be getting access to it earlier than others.

GTA 6 releases at midnight local time around the world. This means you'll be able to start playing it on Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S and PS5 as soon as November 18th turns into November 19th in your region.

The only exception to the rule may be in countries with multiple time zones. For example, Rockstar seems to be classing "midnight" based around the EST time zone in the US, which would mean PST gets it at 9pm on the 18th.

Technically, yes. Due to the staggered rollout, players in New Zealand will be getting first access to GTA 6 at midnight in their time zone, which equates to 11am on November 18th here in the UK, and even earlier in the United States.

We urge caution around this, as Xbox's terms of service specifically state that you shouldn't switch regions unless you're actually located in the country you're switching to, but we'll leave the decision up to you.

News Xbox Fans Urge Caution Over New Zealand Trick For GTA 6, While Others Say It's A Non-Issue

"They literally told me this in person in Seattle at Xbox FanFest last week"

You may have noticed that we didn't mention Xbox One in the release times section up above, and that's because we don't quite know what's happening with it. In a nutshell, Xbox One players will be forced to use Xbox Cloud Gaming in order to get access to GTA 6, which in theory should require buying the game before access is granted.

There are too many unknowns ahead of launch about how this works though. Will cloud access be made available immediately? Will you be able to use the free-with-ads version of the cloud to play GTA 6, or will it require paying for the service? Is it just Xbox One that you can play it on, or will mobile and PC devices be supported too?

That's where we stand ahead of launch, so while GTA 6 definitely will be playable through the cloud on Xbox One in some form, it's probably best to wait until it's been released before handing over any money as things stand.

#4031. How To Unlock First-Person Aiming In GTA 6

First-person mode sadly isn't in GTA 6 proper, but there are some workarounds both in and out of combat.

One of the big gameplay questions surrounding Grand Theft Auto 6 was whether or not it would include a first-person mode like Red Dead Redemption 2 launched with and GTA 5 eventually got.

Sadly, although also understandably, that isn't the case, as GTA 6 doesn't have a full first-person mode to let players see through Jason and Lucia's eyes. There is a way to add it to your guns, though, as well as a similar function.

As soon as you've started Grand Theft Auto 6 and got access to free-roaming, you'll want to head over to any Ammu-Nation on the map, which is marked with a handgun sign. There's one very close to where Jason lives in the Keys, and you'll actually have to visit it as part of an early story mission anyway, so it's impossible to avoid visiting one if you want to progress.

Once you get there, buy any gun that you want, and then select to add an Optics attachment. There are options for close, mid, and long-range optics that will let you zoom in further, but the most basic option costs just $65, so it's something you can get from the very start of the game.

Optics are available for pretty much every type of gun in the game, so don't worry about it being limited to a plain rifle. That being said, you'll have to wait a bit until you can buy some of the advanced guns and really get the customisation going.

If you purchase an Optics attachment for a gun, you can then press R3 while aiming it to enter first-person aiming. Sure, it's not quite what everyone wanted with a first-person mode in GTA 6, but it's the closest thing we've got to it, and it does let you see combat in a more detailed way if that's your preference.

The most anticipated video game of all time is a triumph on every level that exceeds years of unbelievable expectations. You're not ready for Leonida.

Now, while there isn't a full first-person mode in GTA 6, there is a way to more closely inspect things from Jason and Lucia's perspective that doesn't require you to get your gun out and potentially scare people. If you've got nothing equipped, hold down L2 on PS5 and LT on Xbox, and then press in the right stick to "Inspect" the world.

Doing this lets you go into first-person aiming while out of combat, although you can't move around and there's not all that much point to it beyond being able to scan things easily. It does let you see things a bit closer, and can be pretty immersive if you're talking to someone or trying to watch something that's going on in Vice City. Again, it's not exactly first-person mode, but it's better than nothing!

If you want to get around Leonida and clear GTA 6's map with ease, Auto-Drive is one of your best friends.

#4030. Crimson Desert's first patch aims at fixing controls, but it mostly affects mouse and keyboard

The first post-launch patch for Crimson Desert is here, and the list of changes is promising, even if it doesn't go far enough to address some deeper issues.

Crimson Desert has been out for a few days now, and as positive as its been received by many players, the game suffers from several fundamental issues that anyone who’s played it has called out.

Perhaps the loudest one of those has been how the game controls, which is a problem that stems from the complexity of controls themselves, as well as the underlying animations behind many of the actions the player character performs.

In the first case, at least, something is being done.

Developer Pearl Abyss rolled out patch 1.00.03 for Crimson Desert on Monday. The patch is available now on Steam and PlayStation, with Xbox and the Epic Games Store following “at a later time.”

Today’s update follows a letter to players the developer issued on Saturday. The letter generally acknowledged player feedback, but specifically pointed to complaints about the game’s clunky controls as something of a focus for the team.

The action RPG has actually broken its launch peak concurrent player numbers over the weekend, though only by a few thousands more. Its Steam user review rating has also improved over the same period.

This latest update only includes an initial set of fixes, but Pearl Abyss vowed to keep working on addressing all other points of feedback. A highlight in 1.00.03 is the addition of a Storage at Howling Hill Camp, which can be used to store inventory items.

The most important changes, of course, affect how the game controls on keyboard and mouse. Pearl Abyss included several fixes and altered some of the default presets to make the experience less painful when playing the game with a keyboard and mouse.

There are sadly no changes to controllers, but it is something that the developer said we can expect to see in future patches. More improvements for keyboard and mouse setups are in the works, too.

Beyond the control changes, patch 1.00.03 also includes a set of gameplay tweaks, especially when it comes to enemy health and difficulty. It also makes fast travelling more convenient, and brings a few fixes to NPC dialogue. You can read the full change log on Steam.

#4028. Star Wars: Galactic Racer Gets Local Splitscreen Multiplayer Next Year

Star Wars: Galactic Racer has been one of 2026’s breakout titles, but much of the game’s praise stems from its exceptional roguelike single-player mode. If you want to race against human players, you can only do so online. Thankfully, for fans of couch multiplayer, that’s going to change.

Developer Fuse Games announced yesterday that local splitscreen multiplayer is coming to Star Wars: Galactic Racer early next year. The mode lets you race up to three other players on the same screen. That's pretty much all there is to it, but given that local multiplayer was the game's biggest omission and, as a result, the most requested addition, there's probably no better news for Galactic Racer fans.

We’ve heard you! Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to develop a new mode: Free Play. Choose your vehicle, character, planet, and track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local splitscreen action.[image or embed]

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is available now on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC. Read our review of the game here.

#4027. DOOM: The Dark Ages Revelations Gets A Major Free 'Slaughter Mode' Update Today

The release of DOOM: The Dark Ages Revelations saw critics heaping praise on the expansion earlier in 2026, to the point where it's actually even in the Game of the Year (or at least Expansion of the Year) conversation as things stand.

News Xbox Has Another Potential GOTY Candidate On Its Hands, Even Though It's Just DLC

The reviews for Revelations have been absurdly good

The DLC is getting even better today as well, as a new November 16th updating is introducing "Slaughter Mode - an endless combat challenge in which you need to tear through waves of hordes and unlock rewards along the way.

DOOM developer id Software says no two runs in Slaughter Mode are identical due to the random encounters it throws at you, and there will also be special unlockable skins and weekly challenges thrown into the mix.

"Complete rounds to earn Skulls, which unlock rewards such as Slaughter Mode-only Slayer skins, weapon skins for all modes and profile icons. You can also unlock tracks from Andrew Hulshult’s IDKFA soundtrack to play in both Slaughter Mode and the Ripatorium! Take on weekly challenges for more opportunities to earn rewards and show off your slaying prowess."

All of this is available to you if you own the Revelations DLC for DOOM: The Dark Ages already, or if you have the Premium / Premium Upgrade versions of DOOM: The Dark Ages.

Don't forget that the base game is currently included with Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, Premium and PC Game Pass as well, so if you just want the DLC to play on Game Pass, you're looking at paying £17.99 / $19.99 for it.

We'll leave you with more details about the new Slaughter Mode for DOOM The Dark Ages: Revelations below.

Tear through relentless, escalating and unpredictable waves of demonic hordes, carving out your personal best scores and unlocking rewards using the Skulls collected from the carnage. With each checkpoint reached, players must ask themselves if they want to cash in their run or risk it all for more slaughter. No two runs through Slaughter Mode are identical as you fight escalating rounds of random encounters, bosses and arenas, turning up the heat as you proceed further into your run.

#4026. The Blood Of Dawnwalker Just Got A Free 1.2 Update, Adding New Game Plus

The Blood of Dawnwalker is one of the year's biggest, most ambitious games, and the developers over at Rebel Wolves have done a good job cleaning up bugs and performance issues in the weeks since launch. Today, that trend continued; the new 1.2 update is out now on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC, and it adds New Game Plus.

The new mode is uniquely ideal for a game like Dawnwalker. The narrative is very player-driven, whether it has to do with your literal dialogue options, your ability to manage your vampiric hunger, or the order you complete quests, and all of these elements can cause your experience to vary wildly. It makes sense, then, that players would want to jump back in to try things again and see what might happen if the game is played differently, and New Game Plus allows them to do that while keeping combat fresh.

According to the update notes on the Dawnwalker website, "NG+ unlocks after you complete the game’s Epilogue and lets you experience the story again while keeping your progress – mainly your character level, skills, and inventory." You don't gain access to these skills until you complete the prologue, however, which marks the adventure's proper start.

The new mode will also rebalance the world's level scaling. In the base game, certain areas are much harder than others, but in New Game Plus, all enemies will rise in power to match your level, meaning you can explore the world in whatever order you want. On that note, the level cap has also been raised to 100, and protagonist Coen can collect new, more powerful versions of weapons marked with an "NG+" label.

That's basically everything in this update. Rebel Wolves also added some slight tweaks to combat in the base game and adjusted some geometry in the open world, but the main focus here was New Game Plus. This is in contrast to the 1.1 update, which added a much wider suite of bug fixes and made the game run more smoothly.

#4025. How To Enable Auto-Drive In GTA 6

If you want to get around Leonida and clear GTA 6's map with ease, Auto-Drive is one of your best friends.

Unsurprisingly, Grand Theft Auto 6 has an absolutely massive map for the player to explore, with Leonida containing not just Vice City but tons of unique areas and regions with plenty of secrets to uncover.

There's a lot of driving for the player to do in GTA 6, and it can get a little much hopping behind the wheel at every turn, especially if you're trying to see the whole map. There's a way to make things easier, though.

If you've played Rockstar's last game, Red Dead Redemption 2, you might remember that there was an auto-drive function that let you give your horse a waypoint and then automatically head there. Grand Theft Auto 6 picks up this same feature, and it's arguably even more helpful since there's so much ground to cover.

The most anticipated video game of all time is a triumph on every level that exceeds years of unbelievable expectations. You're not ready for Leonida.

Once you've got into a car (or any vehicle, really) and set a waypoint, hold down on the D-Pad and then press the Options button on PS5 and Menu on Xbox, to enter cinematic driving mode. So far, so previous GTA games, but if you then hold down Circle on PS5 or B on Xbox, you'll be able to enable Auto-Drive.

As the name suggests, this causes Jason or Lucia to drive the car to your waypoint for you, and you can even choose a speed to cruise at. Sadly, even the fastest option isn't very fast at all, and auto-driving will cause your character to rigidly follow the rules of the road, so it's not exactly a speedy way to get around the map. It is a good choice if you want to soak in the view and clear the fog of war around Leonida, though.

And don't worry, using auto-drive counts for clearing the map, so you can just set one very long waypoint and see all Leonida has to offer from pretty early on.

First-person mode sadly isn't in GTA 6 proper, but there are some workarounds both in and out of combat.

#4024. Stalker 2’s first expansion officially revealed, and it's taking us to the power plant where it all began

Stalker 2’s first add-on isn’t far off, and it may just be the thing to bring you back to post-apocalyptic Chornobyl in 2026.

One of the biggest reveals out of today’s Xbox Partner Preview showcase has been the new Stalker 2 expansion. The developer did tease some sort of announcement ahead of the event, but I don’t think an expansion was on many of our bingo cards.

Cost of Hope is the big news; a new add-on that the developer has wisely decided to reveal fairly close to release. Or, at least, the planned release target.

First off, Cost of Hope is set for release this summer. It’ll arrive on all current platforms simultaneously, meaning PC, Xbox, and PlayStation. The expansion is described as “non-linear”, and it takes place in the heartlands, deeper into the Zone.

The story revolves around a conflict between Duty, and Freedom, two factions whose idea of the what the Zone is and their understanding of its possibilities differ widely. You’ll be playing as protagonist Skif once again, and the expansion’s events will run parallel to the main game.

GSC Game World says Cost of Hope will introduce two new regions, offering dozens of hours of gameplay. We’ll get to actually explore the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant as part of the expansion, alongside the Iron Forest.

Each of the two new regions will have its own hub area, NPCs, quests, activities and stories. Of course, it wouldn’t be a Stalker expansion without some new weapons, and Cost of Hope promises a few - some can even be seen in the trailer.

The developer also confirmed that there’s one other story DLC in the works. Together with Heart of Chornobyl, and Cost of Hope all three will form a trilogy of interconnected stories. More details on Cost of Hope - including a release date - will be revealed sometime in the summer.

#4023. Sea Of Stars Is Getting A 'Sunset Edition' Switch 2 Physical And A Gorgeous Final Merch Drop

Sabotage Studio's Sea of Stars is no stranger to a physical release or merch drop, and today, iam8bit has announced that it has one final collection in store.

A brand new Switch 2 physical, the Sea of Stars: Sunset Edition ($49.99), is the star of the show, launching on 2nd April 2027. This one packs the full game and all of its expansions on the cartridge (what a concept!), and comes with some sweet sticker sheets and a download code for the game's soundtrack.

There's a beefier option in the Exclusive Edition, which also boasts an exclusive sleeve and an in-box manual, for those after a little throwback.

The beefiest of the bunch, mind you, is still to come. The Collector's Edition contains all of the goodies outlined above, and throws in a bunch of extra merch too. We're talking a double-sided poster, a tote bag, a reversible bandana, a Rainbow Conch keychain, and seven pins, all housed in a Rainbow Conch Chest. Come on, that's sweet.

The Collector's Edition comes in at a pricey $129.99 (or you can just get the merch for $79.99). All of the above are now available to pre-order from the iam8bit website until 11th January, before shipping in April.

As if all of that wasn't enough, iam8bit has also announced that it has two vinyl LPs in the pipeline, one all about the main game soundtrack, and one featuring the tunes from the Throes of the Watchmaker DLC. You'll also find pre-order information about these on the iam8bit site.

#4022. Something Weird Is Going On With GoldenEye 007 And Xbox Game Pass

Earlier this month, you may recall that Xbox announced 14 games that would be leaving Game Pass in early November, with arguably the highlight of the bunch being the classic Rare FPS, GoldenEye 007.

We initially thought this might have been a mistake, but then Xbox doubled-down by announcing the game's departure in an official Xbox Wire roundup, confirming that it would definitely be leaving console and cloud on November 15th.

We're now on November 16th, and GoldenEye 007 remains included with Game Pass. Every other title from the list has been removed from the service, but Bond has defied the odds once again to remain part of the subscription!

So, what's going on here? It might take a while until we find out for sure, but we're going to guess that Xbox has either managed to arrange a deal to keep GoldenEye 007 on Game Pass, or they've just pushed back the removal date.

In any case, it's weird that nobody's said anything about this yet, and we're hoping we'll get clarification in the near future. GoldenEye has always been a game that's been tied up in licensing issues (hence why we never got the cancelled Xbox 360 version of it), but perhaps they've managed to figure out a long-term solution.

Anyway, we'll keep an eye on it, and this article will be updated with any important information that's revealed over the next few days. For now though, feel free to keep enjoying GoldenEye 007 on Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and Premium!

#4021. Never one to lag behind HSR and ZZZ, Genshin Impact will introduce its own new pink-haired animal-themed girl in Version Luna 6

Plus Mondstadt is expanding yet further north in Genshin Impact's Luna 6 update.

Today’s Genshin Impact Special Program has wrapped up, and it’s brought us some big news about the next major update. Luna 6 is the next phase in the action RPG’s story, titled Song of the Welkin Moon: Rondo - Augured Homecoming.

It’s set to arrive on April 8, bringing with it a tonne of new content, including a big expansion to the original region of Mondstadt.

As part of this new update, Mondstadt’s northern parts expand with new areas. The new Dornman Port is one thing, but the most exciting is the Temple of Space. This floating structure is home to Asmoday fragments, and is made up of different realms inspired by Liyue, Sumeru, and various other civilizations from around Teyvat. Launching with the update is a new mechanic that lets you manipulate the space to reveal hidden paths containing secrets.

If you take the time to explore, you’ll find a lot to there to learn about Asmoday, Ruler of Space. There’s a new boss to take on in the temple, too: Watcher: Fallen Vigil.

The only new character in Luna 6 is Linnea, who continues the current trend within HoYoverse games of focussing heavily on cute pink-haired animal-themed girls. Linnea is a 5-Star Geo Bow user who can really work with parties made up of Lunar-Crystallize characters, with her big gimmick being the ability to turn Hydro-Crystallize reactions into Lunar-Crystallize reactions.

Linnea has a companion, Lumi, who allows her to increase the Lunar-Crystallize damage she deals, while also lowering her enemies’ Geo resistance. Linnea can also deliver either off-field Geo damage or a Lunar-Crystallize reaction hit with her Elemental Skill.

Beyond that, she can heal the party using her Elemental Burst. If you take Linnea with you as you explore, she can help you discover rare animals, thanks to her innate naturalist abilities.

This update will also see Chasca get her first-ever rerun, and you’ll be able to roll for her in the first phase of Event Wishes. The second phase will feature no new characters and instead focus on Nefer and Lauma. There’s going to be another Chronicled Wish banner, this time specifically for Fontaine characters.

You can look forward to a few other new arrivals in Luna 6, including The Nod-Krai Trade Expo, some quality of life updates to Miliastra Wonderland to up the number of players in each lobby, not to mention various other UI changes.

Love and Deepspace has kicked off a new event, squarely built around Caleb's new Memory Pair.

Love and Deepspace’s latest update is here, adding a new Memory Pair for Caleb. The event is dubbed Ghosts' Final March, and it’s available now as part of a new Limited Wish Pool, as it has always worked.

The new Memory Pair is a 5-Star Solar-Slot, which can be obtained through the aforementioned Wish Pool. Doing so will unlock the Netherlord Companion for Caleb, and there’s even more for you to explore in this one.

Alongside the big new Memory Pair, Ghosts' Final March also offers the opportunity to earn a new 4-Star Solar-Slot Memory Pair, alongside ten Deepspace Wishes, 500 Diamonds, and other freebies. The event ends on April 11, so you have some time to get in and play.

If you’re only interested in the 5-Star variants, you’ll be happy to know that Infold is sticking with 150 pulls as the absolute maximum to guarantee earning Netherlord. This will be automatically unlocked after you pull both Nether Yearning and Nether Parting through the Wish Pool.

Obtaining either of the two will give you access to all chapters for the new Myth that’s also available as part of this event: Yin Yang Sundering. You can read all the lore once either of the two Memories have been unlocked, and you won’t even need to upgrade either of them.

The Lost Souls event has also kicked off alongside the new update. You can take part to claim a 4-Star Solar Slor Memory Pair for Caleb: Duskshard Dreams and Duskshard Lotus. You can also earn the 3-Star Memory, Lotus Bond, alongside some other freebies like more Wishes, Diamonds, Photo Poses, and an event-exclusive title.

After you unlock Caleb’s Netherlord Companion, you may want to fight alongside him to get another 4-Star Memory for free. You’ll need to challenge the the Rehearsal Stage to do so, and your first clear is guaranteed to get you the Duskshard Lotus Memory.

#4017. Splatoon 3 Version 12.0.0 Update Out Now, Here Are The Full Patch Notes

The dev team also has another update on the way

Update [Wed 18th Nov 2026, 12:05am]: This new update for Splatoon 3 (Version 12.0.0) is now officially available to download. You can see the patch notes below.

Original Story: Nintendo's team-based squid-shooter Splatoon 3 is still going strong, and this week the title is getting updated to Version 12.0.0.

This major update will come with changes to multiplayer, including weapon adjustments. There are also changes to Anarchy Battle, X Battles and challenges. Additionally, there are changes to the GameChat feature on Switch 2. Nintendo also notes how its next update after this one will focus on multiplayer game balance.

You can get the full rundown in the official patch notes below (via Nintendo's official support page):

On this page: Splatoon 3 - Version 12.0.0 (17th November 2026)

Sections marked "on Nintendo Switch 2" apply only to Nintendo Switch 2. All other changes apply to both Nintendo Switch 2 and Nintendo Switch.

Made it possible to participate with a friend in traditional X Battles as a group of two.

Added a feature that allows players to open GameChat and invite friends from their group while playing modes with friends, such as battles or Salmon Run.

This update focuses on making changes to matchmaking and multiplayer balance.

For X Battles, we have added a feature to allow players to play as a pair with a friend. The goal of this feature is to expand the range of ways to play, and we will introduce it on a trial basis starting in Chill Season 2026. After we have introduced it, we will comprehensively analyze how these battles are actually played and how the gameplay situation shifts, including for players who are not playing with a friend. Then we will decide whether to continue providing this feature in future seasons.

For Anarchy Battle (Series), we have changed the matchmaking system such that, in exchange for removing the feature allowing players to continue with the same team, matchmaking will now complete more quickly and with less imbalance of skill level and equipped weapons between players and their opponents.

For Challenges, we have changed how Challenge Power is calculated to make it easier to raise Challenge Power the more wins a player has. With this change, between players who would have ended up with about the same Challenge Power under the previous system, the player who attained the greater number of wins will have the higher final Challenge Power.

For multiplayer balance, we made a variety of changes to main, sub, and special weapons, including changes to the flight distance of Blaster shots.

With most weapons, when a player fires while moving, the player's movement speed is added to the shot's speed to a certain extent, resulting in a more natural trajectory. For Blasters, we have minimized the change in shot flight distance caused by this effect, making it easier to maintain an appropriate distance against an opponent’s Blaster.

Among the special weapons, we have changed the Reefslider because, while there is statistically little impact on victories in matches between extremely skilled players, it has a high impact on matches between less skilled players. The intention behind this change is to alleviate that striking difference. By narrowing the area affected by the explosion we have made it so that players cannot reap the maximum benefit without using it at the precise position. On the other hand, we have extended the invulnerability period to make it harder for opponents who used terrain to survive the explosion to counterattack and easier for the player to make follow-up attacks.

For the Tenta Missiles, we have decreased the vulnerability while firing and expanded the area where it is possible to lock on to opponents. As a result, it will now be easier to use, even in situations where opponents are nearby the player. By decreasing the impact interval, it becomes easier to defeat opponents who are slow to dodge, but the duration for which they must keep dodging is reduced.

We have also added a feature for Nintendo Switch 2 that will make it easier to use GameChat.

The next update will focus on changes to multiplayer balance.

If you haven't already played the game on Switch 2, there's a free upgrade available which includes visual improvements and frame rate optimisations for the platform. In some related news, Splatoon Raiders has also received an eShop demo this week!

#4016. Civilization Developer Firaxis Lays Off A Third Of Its Staff

Firaxis, the studio behind the Civilization series, has laid off around 60 employees, representing a third of its staff. The report comes from Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier.

In a statement provided to Bloomberg by a spokesperson from 2K, a subsidiary of Firaxis' owner, Take-Two, “Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years. As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.”

In addition to the 60 affected staffers, Firaxis studio head Heather Hazen is also departing. Bloomberg also reports, via anonymous Firaxis employees speaking to the outlet, that the studio is working on an unannounced XCOM game that has had a challenging development, with the team recently missing an important development milestone. This project, if it releases, will be the first Firaxis-developed XCOM game since XCOM: Chimera Squad in 2020.

Firaxis’ most recent release is Civilization VII, which launched in February 2025 to favorable reviews but initially "slow" sales, according to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick last August.  The game currently has a Mixed reception on Steam after Firaxis spent the last year updating the game to address player complaints. Before Civilization VII, Firaxis shipped Marvel's Midnight Suns in 2022, another critically well-received game that failed to meet sales expectations.

#4015. After Star Wars Zero Company dev Bit Reactor brought back an unspecified number of furloughed devs, some of those who weren't have seemingly been laid off

"I’m really proud of what we built together"

Early last month, Star Wars Zero Company developer Bit Reactor brought back a number of developers who had been furloughed before the game launched in August. At the time they did not specify how many devs were returning to the studio, with a separate report claiming more than half had become full time staffers again. Unfortunately, it does now seem like not everyone was able to be brought back, with a number of now former workers sharing word of having been laid off.

As spotted by Star Wars outlet Bespin Bulletin, multiple developers shared word of their layoffs to LinkedIn. A producer at Bit Reactor, Michael Blackard was seemingly one of the first to report being laid off, alongside senior QA analyst Ryan Mosher. Ryan Lopez, an environment artist at the studio, shared, "I was laid off from Bit Reactor this week after a three-month furlough, and while it stings, I’m really proud of what we built together." Lopez had apparently been working on the game for more than three years, starting all the way back on the game's pre-production period.

Tyler Eichten, a UI engineer, also said, "As of today, my time with Bit Reactor has come to a close due to a layoff. I am immensely proud of the work that I, the UI/UX team, and the team at large have accomplished. I hope that in this tumultuous industry that my coworkers (and myself) find placement." It's unclear at this point in time if any, or how many, other staffers have been formally laid off, and Bit Reactor are yet to make a comment.

Star Wars Zero Company performed very well both critically and commercially, making it all the more disappointing that not all of those who worked on the game, who made it as great as it seemingly is, get to continue working at the studio. As always, solidarity with all devs affected.

#4014. The Petit Planet beta is coming back with new updates, but you still need to hope for an invite

If you've been missing Petit Planet since it was last available to play, you'll be happy to know that HoYoverse is hosting another test soon.

It’s been quite a while since we’ve heard anything about Petit Planet, the upcoming game from Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail developer HoYoverse. By most accounts, Petit Planet is the studio’s take on Animal Crossing, though with a few interesting ideas of its own.

The game’s most recent test took place all the way back in November, but its next big test isn’t far off.

HoYoverse announced today that Petit Planet’s Stardrift Test is scheduled for April 21. This latest build will be available on PC, Android, and iOS. The beta will include new Neighbors, an updated Starsea Voyage, and more for you to do at the Galactic Bazaar.

Seeing as interacting with Neighbors is a core part of this life sim RPG, the confirmation that new faces will be available in this test is big news. Each Neighbor in Petit Planet is a character, with their own personalty and life story.

The Starsea Voyage now includes a map, too, which you can use to take you to other Islets. If you played any of the previous tests, you should already be familiar with this feature.

The only bit of bad news here is that this remains a closed beta. You’re still encouraged to sign up on the official website, but you’re not guaranteed access. HoYoverse said that only a portion of players who sign up will be invited to the upcoming beta.

Petit Planet remains without a release date. If nothing else, it’ll be interesting to see the progress the game has made since last November’s beta.

#4013. Grand Theft Auto VI Review - Outrageous Fortune

Many superlatives will be heard in the discussion around Grand Theft Auto VI – biggest world, most activities, best graphics, deepest narrative – but its real triumph is the way all those features and others work in service of a cohesive, believable immersion in a criminal fantasy that is hard to grasp until you’ve played it for yourself.

Rockstar’s latest returns players to a dramatically expanded version of the Vice City seen in a prior game, now largely unrecognizable after real and in-game years have passed. Leonida is a joy to explore, filled with a wealth of activities, both mundane and illicit. The game’s design makes many ordinary tasks as compelling as the illegal ones. Go fishing off the boat, brew coffee to wake up, work out at the gym, scuba dive for long-lost treasure, dust crops, motocross in the mud, go dancing at the club. As you move between those activities, the world feels alive with minor events, from traffic accidents to shady individuals a little too interested in your walk to the ATM. GTAVI delights in life's minutiae, with animations, voice lines, and background characters that keep things fresh even dozens of hours into the story. The level of detail everywhere is astounding and, at times, overwhelming. Getting sidetracked is easy.

The focus on detail carries into the visuals. Lucia’s hair blows in the wind, and she absently pushes it back behind her ear. A drug den is littered with paraphernalia and empty containers. A shifty contact quirks a smile – your only hint that things are about to go south. Sweat glistens on your character’s skin after a hard workout, their breathing and heart rate noticeably heightened. Clouds roll together in the sky, creating realistic weather simulations. The commitment to an authentic simulated world is encompassing, thoughtful, and intentional, a testament to hand-crafted and meticulously painstaking development work, paying off in an absorbing play-space that is hard to step away from.

While the day-to-day simulation is fascinating, it also adds pacing and counterpoint to the explosive march of major missions, narrative threads, and set-piece encounters that drive the game forward. Not even one of these meticulously choreographed sequences deserves to be spoiled; they run the gamut from amusing shenanigans at a strip club to intense chases and escapes fueled by raging gunfights and explosions. Many of the best moments leverage an expert sense of musical accompaniment, weaving a slick original score alongside one of the most impressive and wide-ranging licensed soundtracks ever heard in a video game – often to surprisingly emotional effect.

Ranged combat is punchy and enjoyable; smart use of cover and time-slowing focus makes most battles manageable. On-foot navigation is in a similar boat – simple to pick up and uninterested in needless complexity or challenge; the focus is on choosing smart moments for stealth, knowing when to run and when to fight, and selecting the precise instant for a burst of sudden action. Driving is fast and intense, made more appealing by a huge variety of functionally distinct vehicles to enjoy. If there’s a fault to the core and optional story missions, it’s that many feel a bit on rails regarding where to go and what to do at each step. At the same time, that directed approach keeps the pace relentless, and the action and outcomes thrilling. Over many hours, the game morphs and throws new wrenches into the mix at key junctures, teasing and then playing out criminal experiences from petty theft to group heists to illicit spec ops, and punctuates those distinct vibes with memorable and singular moments.

Like its predecessors, GTAVI simultaneously lampoons and celebrates life in modern America, taking aim at targets like social media, wellness lifestyles, rap and music culture, manosphere content, and dozens more. The caricatures land so well because, in many cases, they’re (sadly) barely over the line of the absurdity we see reflected in real life, and because Rockstar so ably captures individual subcultures, dialects, and situations. Behind it all is a scathing critique of wealth inequality and the inherent unfairness of a system that sets most up to fail. It’s a bitter message delivered in honey-wrapped, exhilarating gameplay, but it shines through.

Of all its significant feats, the relationship between Lucia and Jason elevates the game to new heights, lending this installment a heart, tension, and emotional core missing from prior entries. This is, without a doubt, video gaming’s most richly drawn and compelling romance, featuring two leads who are immediately relatable and compelling to watch. Player actions dictate the strength of their bond, deepening the sense of engagement. Like the best crime fiction, you’re left surprised by how much you cheer for two people who regularly commit terrible acts. The two collectively suffer the slings and arrows of a world that always seems stacked against them; the fortune they amass is not a power grab, but a desperate attempt to cling to each other and come out the other side together, and the player can’t help but cheer them on and dread how fate might stand in the way.

Grand Theft Auto VI is a generational game that stands toe-to-toe with many of the great crime stories and satires across other media. It showcases both the entertainment value of interactive play and the current high-water mark for technical and artistic detail in games. Hunt for and count up all the minor faults or foibles you like, but then note how you just spent another hour lost in this remarkable escape into criminality, wanton violence, egregious sex, and the elusive potential of true love.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.
